title: Choosing the turban
hook: young Sikhs decide for themselves how to keep kesh and turban

segments.voice: Yesterday, Punjab's drug crisis, and your line was help them out. Did you offer one kindness without a lecture attached? Today, young Sikhs again, and a choice that's theirs to make. Day one thousand thirty-eight.

Sunday morning. A teenager stands at the bathroom mirror with a long strip of cloth over one shoulder and a phone propped against the tap, playing a tying tutorial at half speed. Fold, wrap, pin, start again. Down the hall, a younger brother still wears a patka, the small cloth their mother ties for him each morning. The teenager could have kept the patka. Could have stopped covering at all. Instead, this morning, the cloth goes round once more, and it holds. Today, how young Sikhs decide for themselves. Choosing the turban.
screen: `A STRIP OF CLOTH AND A TUTORIAL.` → `FOLD, WRAP, PIN, AGAIN.` → `THIS MORNING, IT HOLDS.`

segments.voice: First, what's being kept. Kesh, uncut hair, is one of the five articles of faith. The Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada, asks Sikhs who have taken amrit to keep their hair uncut, and the turban covers and honors it. Second, the choosing. Young Sikhs come to this in different ways. Some grow up in a patka and move to a full turban. Some girls choose a turban, or a keski, a smaller one. Some cut their hair for years and later decide to grow it back. Families argue about it, and pray about it, and still sit down to dinner. The gurdwara door stays open to all of them. Third, why choice matters. Tradition remembers the day Guru Gobind Singh called the Khalsa into being: he asked who would come forward, and one by one, five did. And the Rehat Maryada asks that those who take amrit be old enough to understand what they're promising. The Khalsa begins with a person stepping forward. Fourth, what the choice looks like now. It can mean a tutorial at half speed. It can mean wearing a turban to a new school, or into a job interview, or onto a sports field, and answering the same question politely, again and again. It can mean waiting until you're sure. That's today's line: their choice. Some Sikhs put it this way: a turban tied because you chose it becomes a promise you keep.
screen: `KESH: ONE OF THE FIVE ARTICLES.` · `PATKA, TURBAN, KESKI, OR NOT YET.` · `FIVE STEPPED FORWARD.` · `WORN TO SCHOOL, WORK AND THE FIELD.` · then, large: `THEIR CHOICE.`

segments.voice: Two minutes for someone else's choice. Sit, and let the breath settle. Bring to mind one person who chose something you might not have chosen: what they wear, what they believe, what they gave up, what they took on. Breathe in, and picture them making that decision, maybe at a mirror, maybe late at night. Breathe out, and let go of the urge to vote on it. It's theirs. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Choosing the turban. Young Sikhs deciding for themselves how to keep their uncut hair and whether and how to tie a turban, a choice the tradition wants made with understanding. Today's word.
Your line: their choice. Today, when someone tells you about a decision they made about faith or identity, ask one question to understand it, and offer no verdict. Day one thousand thirty-eight.
